CosmoPulse: Project Summary

On long missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts will be far from real-time medical support, with delayed communication to Earth. CosmoPulse is a health monitoring platform that tracks an astronaut’s condition continuously and alerts both the crew and the ground medical team before small changes become serious problems.

It displays live vitals, including heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, sleep, and stress, and watches for spaceflight-specific risks such as bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, fluid shift, and elevated CO₂. Each astronaut is compared against their own baseline, with green, yellow, or red alerts and trend graphs across mission days.

Cosmo Pulse works offline and syncs when a connection returns. Because medical data is sensitive, it uses encrypted storage, role-based access, and an access log.

Our prototype uses simulated data, with thresholds informed by NASA’s Twins Study and the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).

Technologies: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Chart.js, Python (Flask), AES encryption.
details:
What it does and how it works
CosmoPulse is a health monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long Moon and Mars missions. It tracks heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO₂), body temperature, sleep, and stress in real time, and watches for spaceflight-specific risks such as bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, fluid shift, and elevated CO₂. Instead of relying only on population averages, it compares each astronaut with their own baseline and raises green, yellow, or red alerts with suggested actions, such as rest or exercise. Trend graphs show how health changes across mission days, and a daily risk score gives the crew a quick overview. The prototype runs on simulated data.

Benefits
Astronauts on deep-space missions can face communication delays of up to about 22 minutes each way between Earth and Mars, and onboard medical support is limited. CosmoPulse supports earlier detection of health problems, helps astronauts manage their own health, and gives the ground medical team a clear picture of the crew’s condition. It works offline and syncs when a connection returns.

Intended impact
We want crews to spot and act on health changes before they become emergencies, and to keep sensitive medical data private on missions far from Earth. The same approach could support remote clinics and other isolated environments on Earth.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Chart.js, and Python (Flask), with AES encryption for stored data. We also used AI-assisted development tools to speed up building the prototype. Thresholds are informed by published spaceflight research, including NASA’s Twins Study and the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). No special hardware is required, and the design could later connect to wearable sensors.

Creativity
Most health trackers show averages. CosmoPulse personalizes alerts to each astronaut’s own baseline and combines health monitoring with security: encrypted storage, role-based access for astronauts, flight surgeons, and administrators, and an access log. Medical privacy is often forgotten in space health tools, and we made it a core feature. Its offline-first design also matches the real conditions of deep space.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication delays and unreliable connectivity, so we built offline mode with later sync
  • Privacy and safety of medical data, so we added encryption, access roles, and logging
  • Astronaut autonomy, so alerts include clear, simple recommendations
  • Realism and honesty, so we use research-informed thresholds and state clearly that the data is simulated
  • Usability under stress, so the interface uses simple color-coded status and a short daily risk score
  • Feasibility within the hackathon timeline, so we focused on a working prototype with the most important features
